Paul Krugman writes:

Well, hereâ€™s the thing: regulation demonstrably does work where tort law doesnâ€™t. Consider the environmental issue: in reality, the perpetrators of oil spills never pay most of the cost; but in reality, environmental regulation has led to much cleaner air and water. (Look up the history of Los Angeles smog or the fate of Lake Erie if you donâ€™t believe me.)
So why does regulation work? If polluters can buy off the system ex post, after a disaster, why donâ€™t they manage to totally corrupt regulation ex ante? Thereâ€™s a lot to say about that, and Iâ€™m sure thereâ€™s a literature I havenâ€™t read. But one thing we tend to forget in this age of Reagan is the importance and virtues of a dedicated bureaucracy: when you have professional government agencies with a job to do, and treat them with respect, that job often gets done.

I'll offer a few points:
1. Here is Susan Rose-Ackerman on regulation vs tortÂ (JSTOR).Â  This is a standard piece in the area, and although she does not stress public choice arguments, the upshotÂ is not extremelyÂ far from Krugman's conclusions.Â Â She thinks that tort can replace regulation to only a limited degree.
2.Â I agree with Krugman that the "tort only" position espoused by some libertarians does not work.Â  Yet I do not think his remarks are pointing at the best possible understanding of the question.Â  For instanceâ€¦
3.Â There is in fact an agency regulating off-shore drilling and in the case under question it totally failed.Â  How can Lake Erie, an orthogonally related success,Â be cited butÂ this very directly relevant failureÂ not be mentioned?Â  
FurthermoreÂ standard accounts of this failure blame regulatory capture, and the Congressional desire for revenue for this failure, not the ideology of free market economics.Â  You might also blame voter sentiment, since Obama seemed to pick up some advocacy of off-shore drilling from the Republicans and arguably this happened because that position proved to be one of the few effective Republican arguments in the last election.Â  
4. There are plenty of problems where tort works better than regulation, most notably when behavior cannot be controlled or measured easily ex ante or where the correct decision relies on the producer's decentralized information.Â  This encompasses numerous areas, fromÂ medical practices to accident law to injuries resulting from the handling of guns to, most of all,Â many micro-components of highly regulated sectors.Â Â Here is a legal and moral defense of tort law.
5. Off-shore drilling is closely related to these cases.Â  For a number of obvious reasons, it is hard for the regulator to monitor how safe an off-shore platform really is.Â  We thus relyÂ a lot on ex post penalties in this area (regulatory as well as tort), not because of ideology but because the ex ante proscriptions don't have as much bite as we would like.Â  This reliance on the ex post penalty also means that "regulation plus tort" (never mind "regulation alone" or "tort alone") may not work so well in this area, with or without free market ideology.
6. Krugman seems to argue that regulators are more protected from the ravages of bad ideology than are judges.Â  Maybe yes, maybe no (see below), but such a comparative argument isÂ unnecessary.Â  TheÂ most salientÂ pointÂ for Krugman's conclusion is simply that optimality requires a bit of regulation and a bit of tort law and that to do without regulation is, in some regards, to be too lax.Â Â He could justify his main conclusion much more simply than he does.Â  (That said, I still believe inÂ less regulation than Krugman does, though I accept the logic of this argument.)
7. If we need to make the said comparison â€“Â the corruptibility of regulation vs. the corruptibility of tort law â€“Â an independent judiciary need not do worse than a respected bureaucracy and indeed the former is arguably more protected from political interference.Â  It's also the case that the judiciary is more likely to overturn very bad behavior from other parts of the government.Â  This is an advantage for judicial approaches over reguatory approaches and it is a further sign of (partial) judicial independence.
8.Â I worry whenÂ numerous bloggers and writers â€” not just Krugman â€” hold aÂ primary theory of regulatory failure based onÂ regulators who do not agree with them ideologically.Â  This isÂ at odds with a big chunk of the relevantÂ public choice literature, which stresses knowledge and incentives, yet without ruling out ideological bias as a factor.Â Â Political science approaches to regulation offer greater scope for ideological bias as a major cause of regulatory failure, but stillÂ it is hardly the dominant theory to the exclusion of others.Â  In this matter we should follow the literature, and evidence, which are there for the taking.
title: Regulation vs. tort

An essential step to see if this view has ground is analysing how multinational banks have been faring in the months of the crisis, in comparison to domestic banks. The case, Lewis v. Chicago, involved alleged discrimination against African American applicants for the Chicago Fire Department who took a test in 1995.

Arnold Kling makes some good points:

â€¦after a crash it is very tempting for people to believe that the previous prosperity was false. However, there is a good economic case for presuming that it is a recession that is an aberration, not prosperity. For example, a graph of long-term GDP growth shows a steady upward trend, to which we return even after severe recessions. 
We still have the capacity to produce the output we produced in 2006. Therefore, to a first approximation, we should still be able to consume what we consumed in 2006. 

I have a few responses:
1. The problem is not in reattaining the 2006 level per se, but rather that people in 2006 expected an entire future path of growth which now appears further away.Â  They made plans based on these expectations and we are not yet in a position to make comparably luxurious plans.Â  Ireland is an extreme example of this point and do note that their capital stock has not been destroyed.
2. As I've written elsewhere, I remain anÂ optimist about the future path of utility, though perhaps not gdp.Â Â ManyÂ of today's innovations improve people's lives directly, without necessarily generating much revenue or employment.
3. This problem also resembles the equity premium issue.Â  Each crisis there is some probability that "this time is different" and upward growth will not resume or at least not for a long time.Â  Until that expectation is cleared away (if indeed it is cleared away), the real living standard is genuinely lower, most of all in expected value terms.
4. I'm still an optimist about the much longer run, whether for utility or gdp.Â  In fact the greater the current labor market troubles, the greater the long-run "human capital dividend" from reallocating resources.Â  Sooner or later, we'll have another burst of important innovation, comparable to that of 1870-1940.Â  We just don't have it now.

Here is an interview with Joshua Coval, of Harvard Business School,Â about his current research.Â  I would urge caution on interpreting these results, but this is what the data toss back out at us:

Q: One of your findings was that the chairs of powerful congressional committees truly bring home the bacon to their states in the forms of earmark spending. Can you give a sense of how large this effect is?
A: Sure. The average state experiences a 40 to 50 percent increase in earmark spending if its senator becomes chair of one of the top-three committees. In the House, the average is around 20 percent. For broader measures of spending, such as discretionary state-level federal transfers, the increase from being represented by a powerful senator is around 10 percent.
Q: Perhaps the most intriguing finding, at least for me, was the degree and consistency to which federal spending at the state level seemed to be connected with a decrease in corporate spending and employment. Did you suspect this was the case when you started the study?
A: We began by examining how the average firm in a chairman's state was impacted by his ascension. The idea was that this would provide a lower bound on the benefits from being politically connected. It was an enormous surprise, at least to us, to learn that the average firm in the chairman's state did not benefit at all from the increase in spending. Indeed, the firms significantly cut physical and R&D spending, reduce employment, and experience lower sales.
The results show up throughout the past 40 years, in large and small states, in large and small firms, and are most pronounced in geographically concentrated firms and within the industries that are the target of the spending.

For the pointer I thank Alex Prado.
Addendum: Megan McArdle comments on the difficulty of interpretation.

My favorite sight has beenÂ the mother-daughter pair I saw on the Bosporous ferry.Â  They were hugging each other on the benchÂ and had virtually the same profile features, yet the mother carriedÂ full traditional dress and the daughter wore a mini-skirt and was otherwise dressed comparably.Â  They loved each other dearly.
How you interpret these women is central to how you view Istanbul.Â  One intuition is that they are quite alike, another is that they are quite different.
And the food?Â Â You can eat the traditional dishes, in simpler settings,Â or you canÂ payÂ extra to eat them â€” slightly modified â€” in more gussied up surroundings.Â  The key to eating well here is to go simple and to look for the best andÂ purest versions of straightforwardÂ dishes.Â Â World class raw ingredients are at your disposal, if only you don't let anyone ruin them.
It's not hard to find the good stuff.Â  Thousands of street restaurants offer seafood (the fried small smelts are my favorite, then the sea bream or "levrek"), eggplants, fava beans, doner kebab, fried mussels, salads with cheese and tomatoes, lamb brains, fried and baked potatoes, Turkish ravioli (harder to find), spicy kabob with sumac, andÂ other delicacies.Â  It is common for the small restaurants to specialize, an indication of quality.Â  AÂ meal in these places, with one small portion, will cost six to ten dollars but you can (and should) order more.Â  Turkish sweets are theÂ dessert and I preferÂ something with pistachio.
The rest is a sideshow.Â  Avoid all restaurants near the main sights or near clusters of tourist hotels.Â  Avoid most of the places â€” even Turkish ones â€” on the main thoroughfares.Â  Look for the neighborhood side streets with clusters of these small restaurants, just off the larger roads.Â Â If you order small dishes, you can visit two or three restaurants in one meal, no problem.
My favorite small Istanbul restaurants have beenÂ the soup houses, especially the tripe soup (NB: you don't have to like most tripe dishes to enjoy these creations).Â  You ladle inÂ some liquid garlic sauce, paprika, a bit of chili pepper, and aÂ green herb of some kind.Â  Some of these places are open for breakfast.
Unless you've bled this cityÂ dry and sampled all the major dishesÂ (which would take a longÂ time), the return to going upscale, or seeking innovation,Â is not overwhelming.Â  What happens is thatÂ you're either paying higher prices to be in the company of attractive Turkish women or to impress attractive Turkish women who are already inÂ your company.Â  Not that there's anything wrong with that, but the basic market model here is segregation of restaurant type.Â Â If it's food you're after, don't payÂ more for the culinary twists.Â Â The foodÂ will remain recognizably Mediterranean but it won't beÂ the classic treatment you are looking for and which to you isÂ still original on the fifth day of your trip.
If your restaurant has a good number of attractive Turkish women in it, perhapsÂ you made a food mistake.Â  Or should I say a money mistake?Â  Or what kind of mistake?Â  TheÂ cuisine still will beÂ good.
The good here is very good and the best isn't that much better.Â

Since the mid-1980s, cigarette-smoking policies have become increasingly restrictive in jails and prisons across the United States. Cigarette black markets of various form and scale often emerge in jails and prisons where tobacco is prohibited or banned. Case studies of 16 jails and prisons were undertaken to understand the effects of cigarette bans versus restrictions on inmate culture and prison economies. This study describes how bans can transform largely benign cigarette â€œgray markets,â€� where cigarettes are used as a currency, into more problematic black markets, where cigarettes are a highly priced commodity. Analysis points to several structural factors that affected the development of cigarette black markets in the visited facilities: the architectural design, inmate movement inside and outside, officer involvement in smuggling cigarettes to inmates, and officer vigilance in enforcing the smoking policy. Although these factors affect the influx of other types of contraband into correctional facilities, such as illegal drugs, this study argues that the demand and availability of cigarettes creates a unique kind of black market.

text:
Matt Yglesias writes:

We right now have the capacity to produce moreâ€“much moreâ€“than has ever been produced before in the history of the planet. There are dozens of supply-side policies that could be improved in every country on earth, but thatâ€™s not a new fact about the world. Whatâ€™s new is the lack of demand, the willingness of the key leaders in Tokyo, Frankfurt, Washington, Berlin, and now it seems London as well to tolerate stagnation and disinflation in the face of some of the most exciting fundamental new opportunities for human economic betterment ever. 

You can take that quotation as a stand-in for the more general Keynesian AD views about the current recession.
First, I am fully on board with Scott Sumner-like ideas to boost AD through monetary policy, as is Yglesias and are many other Keynesians.Â  There is no practical disagreement, but it remains an open question how effective such measures (or a bigger stimulus) would be.Â  
Consider a simple model, in which uncertainty goes up, first because of the U.S. financial crisis,Â now because of Greece and the Euro and the open questions about Spain and how well Europe can cooperate.Â  I'm not saying that's the only or even the prime cause of what's going on, it's simplyÂ an illustrative story.
With higher uncertainty, investors pull back, wait,Â and exercise option value.Â  Aggregate supply declines, as does employment.Â  As a result, aggregate demand declines too, and that includes real aggregate demand, not just nominal aggregate demand.Â  Until the underlyingÂ uncertainty is resolved, the economy remains in the doldrums.
Note that there is still a case for fiscal policy, based on the idea of intertemporal substitution.Â  With some labor unemployed, a sufficiently finely targeted fiscal policy can build a new road at lower social cost than before, by drawing upon unemployed resources.Â  But even if that fiscal policy is a good idea, it won't drive recovery, at least not for plausible values of the multiplier.
There is also still a case for countercyclical monetary policy.Â  As real AS and real AD are falling (see above), there is alsoÂ downward pressure on nominal variables.Â  Aggressive monetary policy, or for that matter the velocity-accelerating aspect of fiscal policy, can limit the negatives of this process and check the second-order fall in employment.
I'm all for countercylical AD management, noting that for other reasons I prefer monetary to fiscal policy in most cases and even if you don't agree with me there it suffices to note that the monetary authority moves last in any case.
ThatÂ all said, the countercyclical monetary policy won't drive recovery either, or set the world right again, it just limits the damage.Â  WeÂ still have to wait for the uncertainty to be cleared up.Â 
Reading the Keynesian bloggers, one gets the feeling that it is only an inexplicable weakness, cowardice, stupidity, whatever, that stops policies toÂ drive a more robust recovery.Â Â The Keynesians have no good theory of why their advice isn't being followed, except perhapsÂ that the Democrats are struck with some kind of "Republican stupidity" virus.Â  (This is also an awkward point for Sumner, who seems to suggest that Bernanke hasÂ forgotten his earlier writings on monetary economics.)Â  The thing is, that same virus seems to be sweeping the world, including a lot of parties on the Left.
Romer, Geithner, Summers, et.al. know all the same economics that Krugman andÂ DeLong and Thoma do.Â  If a bigger AD stimulus would set so many things right, they'd gladly lay tons of political capital on the line to see it through and proclaim triumph at the end of the road.
Except they expectÂ it would bring only a marginal improvement.Â  And for that marginal improvement they have only a marginal desire to:
1. Raise the long-term national debt (if it's fiscal stimulus)
2. Put their reputations behind policies which might backfire or irritate Congress,
3. Put additional pressure on the independence of the Fed (if it's more aggressive monetary policy)
4. Wreck the current term spread of interest rates, which is a) making the short-term debt easy to finance, and b) restoring major banks to profitability rather quickly.
I still think they should try to do it â€” through more aggressive monetary policy â€” but it's a judgment call and that's why they are more or less staying put.
In general you should be suspicious of explanations which take the form of "if only the good people would all band together and get tough."Â

But despite all this, there's one pretty good reason to think that Tyler is basically right: tax cuts. Lefty economists might generally believe that increasing spending is a more efficient way of stimulating consumption than reducing taxes, but they'd almost certainly accept a big tax cut as an almost-as-good substitute. And tax cuts have two big advantages over spending. On the substantive side, they work faster. Spending takes time to work its way through the economy, but a tax cut (for example, a payroll tax holiday) boosts the economy almost immediately. And on the political side it's quite doable. Republicans would be persuadable because they love tax cuts and Democrats would be persuadable because it would help the economy. For Obama, then, it would be the best of all worlds: a fast stimulus that gets bipartisan support, something that boosts the economy while dampening the inevitable criticism he'd get for blowing up the deficit.
But he's not pushing for this. Not even quietly. And this suggests that Tyler is right: Obama's advisors might be in favor of further fiscal stimulus, but not by much. And the best explanation for this is that lefty or not, they're genuinely afraid, as Tyler says, that it would bring only marginal improvements at the cost of significant problems down the road.

Matt and Ezra both comment on my post that most ofÂ the largest Chinese firms are state-owned or controlled by state-owned banks.Â  (Both blogs, by the way, have interesting running coverage of the same China trip.)Â  How can this be the case in the world's greatest economic growth miracle?Â  How come it works (sort of, there were lots of privatizations, starting in the 1980s) in France too?
Yet state-owned industries do not have a fantastic record overall; ask England.
In part this is a puzzle but in part France and China have one importantÂ feature in common: it'sÂ high status to be a ruler.Â  Very smart Frenchmen often grow up wanting to work for the government.Â  Hardly anyone in France thinks that is weird and soÂ the French bureaucracy has some of the best talent in the country.
There is also a long-standing tradition of the prestige of the Chinese mandarin.Â  Furthermore, and perhaps more importantly, the Chinese Communist Party is the ultimate source of control and prestige for the entire society and it too attracts many talented people.Â  
It's not enough to attract talented people, however.Â  Unlike in the former communist Soviet Union, the Chinese government is (somewhat) dedicated to improving the nation.Â  At least at a ten percent rate of growth, this political equilibrium works.Â  And the state-controlled enterprises have to compete in a commercial environment, again unlike many former socialist experiments with state ownership.Â  Most of all, China is grabbing the low-hanging fruit by moving smart, hard-workingÂ individuals from rural jobs to highly productive jobs and when you are grabbing the low-hanging fruit many things are possible.Â Â A lot of systems work OK until you get near the "you ought to shut down" constraint.
It's also possible that the successes of state ownership "decay" with time, as was arguably the case with the French model before the privatizations and has been the case with NASA in the United States.
The United States is far from having the right pieces to make public ownership work on a widespread basis and of all the major capitalist economies we haveÂ experimented with it about the least.Â  Federalism, a regionalist Congress, separation of powers, and a high proportion of political appointees all militate against successful government ownership.Â  Plus we are a large economy with relatively little external discipline in the form of international trade.
We could "respect" our bureaucrats much more than we do, yetÂ they still would not have the real status they enjoyÂ in France.Â  It's simply not built into our culture, which worshipsÂ wealthy businessmen and alsoÂ the so-called "common man."
Imagine if everyone wrote a tweet: "Hey guys, over at the Department of Education.Â  You're awesome. Luv ya!"Â  It wouldn't much matter because still notÂ many peopleÂ deeply and sincerely wish to emulate them.
I also prefer to live in a society where the public sector does not have so much prestige.Â  Very often governmental prestigeÂ stifles innovation and implies a series of more general insider, elitist, and sometimes authoritarianÂ attitudes.Â  It's also worth a quick look at the histories of what France and China had to do to build up so much governmental prestige; not pretty.
We should recognize that the public ownership model has worked for China, butÂ I don't want to see it widely copied.Â  I don't want to see it in Venezuela, Argentina, Turkey, Pakistan, Sri Lanka,Â Cuba, India, the Philippines,Â Nigeria, Central African Republic, or anywhere in Eastern Europe, to nameÂ a few other candidate countries.Â  Do you?
title: When does large-scale public ownership work?

Brad DeLong writesÂ (do read his entire post on my post, it is too long to excerpt; also read the comments on his post):

In this environment, an increase in uncertaintyâ€“a mean-preserving spreading-out of ex ante investment project return distributionsâ€“causes a greater share of investment projects to fail to make the 1/ÃŽÂ² guaranteed gross-rate-of-return hurdle. So production of investment goods fallsâ€¦
â€¦and production of consumption goods rises, as labor is redirected. 
There is no employment-reducing fall that I can see in aggregate supply in response to an increase in uncertainty. Yes, there is a structural readjustment as investment-goods industries shed labor and consumption-goods industries gain labor. But this is no more a fall in aggregate supply that leaves an extra 5% of the labor force with nothing productive to do than there was a fall in aggregate supply earlier, when perceived uncertainty fell and labor moved into investment-goods productionâ€“remember, back when financial engineering guaranteed by S&P and Moody's offered a way to create more of the AAA assets that the representative worker wanted to hold. There is a fall in aggregate supply in the sense that the value added by investment projects fallsâ€“but that fall shouldn't have implications for employment.

I think Brad is assuming I've fallen into the "Paul Krugman is right and Austrian Business Cycle theory is wrong" trap, but it's a different story.Â  I have in mind a model of costly-to-reverse investment where many entrepreneurs decide to wait.Â  It's also the case that producing consumption goods can be risky, even non-durable consumption goods:Â look at the decline in the number of luxury food items in a Whole Foods over the last few years.Â  Brad may not be convinced, but there's no logical problem in the story.
Here is one of the empirical pieces on how uncertainty reduces investment and yes RW this is also a negative supply shock, as it makes extantÂ resources less productive, at least for the time being.Â  Here are more papers in the area.Â  Here is one recent relevant modelÂ or see the papers of Robert Pindyck.Â  Again, I don't wish to push "uncertainty" as the only story, it's rather the simplest means of seeing that it's not all just about weak aggregate demand.
Scott Sumner likes to scream from the rooftops about how Bernanke has forgotten his previous work on monetary economics.Â  I like to note that there is more than one â€” indeed more than two â€” Ben Bernankes.Â  He wrote his MIT dissertation on uncertainty and irreversible investment.Â  One of the Ben Bernankes I follow is in part a real business cycle theorist.
Brad also writes:

â€¦the cost of borrowing for the government has fallenâ€“the market value troday of future cash tax flow earmarked for debt repayment has gone way, way upâ€“therefore we should dedicate more future cash flow to debt repayment by borrowing more. There is no "but even." Expansionary fiscal policy is a good idea.

I'll blog more on that soon, in a separate post.Â  For the time being I'll repeat my point that the monetary authority moves last anyway, so it's ultimately a matter of monetary rather than fiscal policy, whether we like that fact or not.

text:
Mark Thoma writes:

As for Tyler's (and others') call for monetary policy instead of fiscal policy, here's the problem. It relies upon changing expectations of future inflation (which changes the real interest rate). You have to get people to believe that the Fed will actually be willing to create inflation in the future when it comes time to do so. However, it's unlikely that it will be optimal for the Fed to cause inflation when the time comes. Because of that, the best policy is to promise that you'll create inflation, then renege on the promise when it comes time to follow through. Since people know that, and expect the Fed will not actually carry through, it's hard to get them to change their expectations now. All that credibility the Fed has built up and protected concerning their inflation fighting credentials works against them here.

This makes perfect sense in terms of a model, but I don't seeÂ inflationary expectations as the relevant factors for the real world.Â  Let's say the government/central bank prints up rebate checks and mails them around.Â  People either spend those checks or they don't.Â  If the checks are spent, AD goes up and the policy more or less succeeds.
If people don't spend the checks, they are engaging in "balance sheet repair."Â  In absolute terms, things are going less well than in the previous scenario, but still they're going as well as possible, given the dour expectations.Â  Balance sheet repair probably is needed and it is preparation for a later expansion, once the repairs are finished.Â  The policy still isÂ "as successful as a policy can be."Â  (The alternative of fiscal policy won't have much of a multiplier and the higher debt may cause some more balance sheet worry.)
Which scenario will come to pass?Â  I doubt if it has much to do with the expected rate of inflation, or changes in real interest rates, at least not within normal U.S.Â ranges for those variables.Â  It probably has more to do with overall sentiment, indebtedness, joblessness, and so on.Â  A non-credible Fed, when it comes to the rate of future price inflation,Â need not crush the possibility that the funds will be spent.Â  I don't trust the Fed, or the ECB for that matter, and last night we went out for dinner.
Keep also in mind that balance sheet repair does not require currency holdings.Â  (Keynes is clear on currency vs. savings, but I'm not sure the current debates always are.)Â  Saved funds go to the bank.Â  The bank may or may not make more loans, and spur more investment and durables purchases, but we're no longer in a position where financial intermediaries are "broken."Â  The additional lending, whileÂ it's hardly guaranteed,Â could indeed happen and that would occur at the same time as balance sheet repair.Â  What a nice outcome.Â  Again, it is not obvious to me that the expected rate of price inflation, or expected real intereest rates, areÂ major factors in determining how well this goes; I would again look to the overall state of expectations, including how much uncertainty there is.Â  I'll blog a bit more soon on why real interest rates don't always matter so much.
Even if it does come down to credible expectations, perhaps people only need to believe that the Fed will continue expansionary policy if unemployment remains high.Â  If a recovery is booming, expectations can allow for the Fed to contract a bit, because the first-order influence of all those positive income effects is so high.Â  Let's say you thought the Fed would contract as we approached macro-near-Nirvana and that was coming in three years' time.Â  I still think you'd be willing to spend your rebate check today.
I'm all for credible central banks, I just don't thinkÂ that is currently the missing ingredient.
title: What does successful monetary policy require?

text:
In the WSJ online I cover Hollywood and capitalism including Star Wars, Star Trek, Avatar, The Wire and much else.Â  Here are two bits:
Although Hollywood does sometimes produce leftist films like "Reds," it has no deep love for socialismâ€¦
But Hollywood does share Marx's concept of alienation, the idea that under capitalism workers are separated from the product of their work and made to feel like cogs in a machine rather than independent creators. The lowly screenwriter is a perfect illustration of what Marx had in mindâ€“a screenwriter can pour heart and soul into a screenplay only to see it rewritten, optioned, revised, reworked, rewritten again and hacked, hacked and hacked by a succession of directors, producers and, worst of all, studio executives. A screenwriter can have a nominally successfully career in Hollywood without ever seeing one of his works brought to the screen. Thus, the antipathy of filmmakers to capitalism is less ideological than it is experiential. Screenwriters and directors find themselves in a daily battle between art and commerce, and they come to see their battle against "the suits" as emblematic of a larger war between creative labor and capital. 

On The Wire:

	â€¦although it uses character, "The Wire" is ultimately about how character is dominated by larger economic forces: drug dealers come and go, but the drug market is forever. "Capitalism is the ultimate god in The Wire. Capitalism is Zeus," says David Simon, the show's creator.


	Over its five seasons, "The Wire" shows how money and markets connect and intertwine white and black, rich and poor, criminal and police in a grand web that none of them truly comprehendsâ€“a product of human action but not of human design. It's the invisible hand that's calling the shots, as Mr. Simon subtly reminds us in the conclusion to the third season, when Detective McNulty wondrously pulls a book from the shelf of murdered drug dealer Stringer Bell, and the camera focuses in on the title: "The Wealth of Nations" by Adam Smith.


	Smith's metaphor of the invisible hand, like Mr. Simon's invocation of Zeus, tells us that to understand the world we need to look beyond the actions of individuals to see the larger forces at work. But Zeus is an arbitrary and capricious god whose lightning bolts fall out of the sky without reason or direction. Smith's "invisible hand," however, is that of a kinder god, a god that cares not one whit for individuals but nevertheless guides self-interest toward the social good, progress, and economic growth. So Mr. Simon understands that the Baltimore dockworkers lost their jobs because of the relentless change that capitalism brings and not through any fault of their own. But Adam Smith sees what Mr. Simon does not, namely that it was capitalism that brought the Baltimore stevedores their high wages in the first place and it is the relentless change of capitalism that slowly raises wages throughout the world. 

More here.

text:
Let's look again atÂ Brad DeLong on fiscal policy:

The U.S. Treasury can borrow for thirty years, taking all CPI risk onto its own books, and pay only 1.83% per year in interest?
Wow.
Ahem.
It's not just that a greater amount of government investment meets the benefit-cost test when the government can borrow at 1.83% in inflation-proof bonds for thirty years, a whole bunch of tax postponements do as well. And so do a whole bunch of expanded social welfare programs. And so do a whole bunch of government issues of debt which are then invested in risky private ventures.
â€¦the cost of borrowing for the government has fallenâ€“the market value today of future cash tax flow earmarked for debt repayment has gone way, way upâ€“therefore we should dedicate more future cash flow to debt repayment by borrowing more. There is no "but even." Expansionary fiscal policy is a good idea,

To explain why I view it differently, let's start with a parable from the private sector.Â  Managers in large corporations oftenÂ are given project "hurdle rates" of twenty to thirty percent, not because their cost of capital is so high, but because of agency problems.Â  If the manager were given a hurdle rate of eight percent, he or she mightÂ go crazy with new projects and the companyÂ would too easily meet its ruin.Â  It then follows that changes in the actual cost of capital, within moderate ranges, don't so much influence private investment and in this second or third best sense shouldn't.Â  If the hurdle rate is thirty percent, and the cost of capital falls from ten to seven percent for a business, that maybe looks like a bigÂ changeÂ but actually it's a change in a largely non-binding constraint.
All that is standard and it has long been stressed by Joseph Stiglitz, among others. Furthermore in regressions the cost of capital often fares poorly in predicting private sector investment and that is one reason why.Â  I don't regard the above as "proven" but it does seem to be "likely."
Now let's turn back to the government.Â  Pre-crash, it already could borrow at low real rates of interest.Â  And there already wereÂ unexploited public sector projects with high potential rates of return.Â  But we don't want our government to go crazy, spending moneyÂ without limit.Â  There are agency problems and a lot of the money ends up spent poorly.Â  We instead wish to impose a hurdle rate on government projects.Â  Let's say we trust our government more than shareholders trust private sector managers.Â  That could mean a government project hurdle rate of, say, fifteenÂ percent, which would be below the typical private sector hurdleÂ rate.Â  I'm being generous in that comparisonÂ of course; note that mistaken private sector projects get reversed more easily, through bankruptcy,Â than governmental mistakesÂ do.
OK, there's a hurdle rate of fifteenÂ percent and the cost of capital to government falls from three percent to one percent.Â  How much does it matter?Â  Should it matter?Â Â The hurdle rate â€” the most binding constraint â€” hasn't changed.
There are many ways of complicating and modifying this model, and I am not saying that the correct "elasticity of projects," with regard to the real interest rate should be zero.Â  Still, I think this model explains why I am less impressed with the real interest rate changes than isÂ Brad.
There is the separate â€” and very important issue â€” of covering for the worst-case scenarios.Â  This is stressed, correctly, in analyses of global warming but it matters in fiscal policy too.
One could make the quite different argument that we today have a better administration than average and that therefore the hurdle rate should be lower and government spending should be higher.Â  Now is not the time or place to evaluate such claims, but in terms of logic that to me is a stronger argument than citing the real interest rate effect.Â  It focuses on the most binding constraint, namely the hurdle rate stemming from the agency problems.Â  At the same time, it is an argument for higher spending with or without Keynesian factors or unemployed resources playing a major role.Â  It's the common sense point that a more competent manager should undertake more tasks.
title: Should government be spending more when real interest rates are low?

Fresh off of the most substantial national liquidity crisis of the last generation and the enactment of sweeping credit card regulation in the form of the Credit CARD Act, Congress continues to deliberate, with a continuing drumbeat of support from lobbyists, a set of new regulations for credit card companies. only case- or region-specific. By examining 11,135 global fisheries, we
found a strong link: By 2003, the fraction of ITQ-managed fisheries
that were collapsed was about half that of non-ITQ fisheries. This
result probably underestimates ITQ benefits, because most ITQ fisheries
are young.
The results of this analysis suggest that well designed catch shares
may prevent fishery collapse across diverse taxa and ecosystems.

One of the authors of the paper, Christopher Costello, is featured in the video below from Reason TV which covers the world wide decline in fish stocks, "capital stuffing," and the use of ITQs to solve the tragedy of the commons (FYI, all these concepts are discussed in Modern Principles).
The video mentions but does not investigate further the problem of fish and whales that travel long distances, making property rights more difficult to enforceâ€“a good subject for classroom discussion. See also this 60 Minutes video on tuna. 
Addendum: Catch-shares have recently (2009) been introduced in Cape Cod.Â  Here's a good primer on the costs, benefits and difficulties of implementation.Â  One interesting observation: 
Doing away with season restrictions reduces 'derby' conditions, in which fishermen race out, even in dangerous weather, to catch as much as possible. It also eliminates seasonal market gluts, potentially increasing the prices fishermen can command for their catch.

I'm writing to thank so many of you for your interest in Modern Principes: Microeconomics, Modern Principles: Macroeconomics, and the two-in-one edition.Â  Alex and I have been pleased to see how many of you have adopted the book or shown interest in it; all the books are doing great and thanks to your interest.Â  Translations to other languages are already in the works.
Here are a few of my favorite things Modern Principles:
1. It has the most thorough treatment of the interconnectedness of markets and the importance of the price system; most texts only pay lip service to this.

3. It has an entire chapter on ethics and economics.Â  We do present economics as a value-free science, yet we all know how much ethics shapes people's economics views.Â  The book helps the student sort out common confusions and explains the ethical presuppositions behind many "economic" arguments.

5. International examplesâ€“from Algeria to Zimbabweâ€“are written into the core of the book and not just ghettoized in a single "international chapter."
6. It is obsessed with the idea of teaching students to think like economists.
7. It is grounded in the belief that reading an economics text should be fun, not a chore.
8. It has balanced coverage of neo-Keynesian and real business cycle approaches.
9. It covers Solow "catch-up" growth, and Paul Romer's increasing returns, much more thoroughly than do the other texts.Â  The macro book (section) starts off with the idea of why growth matters and is central to macroeconomics.

In 1984, my marriage to Cindy was in serious trouble. I had started once a week therapy with a McLean Hospital based psychiatrist named Lenore Boling, and I used the sessions really just to give voice to my unhappiness with what my relationship with Cindy had become. Despite the unhappiness, I do not think I ever shed a tear in those sessions over the shambles of the marriage. One day, however, I started talking about my work. I tried to explain to Dr. Boling that in all of my writing, whether it was on Kant's First Critique or Hume's Treatise or Das Kapital, my goal always was to plumb the depths of the author's central idea and recast it in a form so simple, so clear, so transparent that I could hold it before my students or my readers and show them its beauty. As I said these words, tears started to well up in me, and I finally had to stop talking because I could not finish. It was the only time in twenty years of psychotherapy that I cried openly in a session. Ever since that day, twenty-five years ago, I have understood that it is this intellectual intuition of the transparent beauty of an idea, not the desire for status or recognition or money, that has throughout my life been the driving force behind my writing and teaching. This is why it makes little difference to me whether reviewers agree with what I say, and it is why I am made somewhat uncomfortable by praise. The intrinsic beauty of the idea is the focus of my concern. It seems that I am, after all, more capable of shedding tears for the central argument of the Deduction of the Pure Concepts of Understanding than I am for a failed marriage or even for a deceased parent. I am not at all sure that is admirable, but it is closer to the truth about myself than I have ever come before.

That's from Robert Paul Wolff, hat tip goes to The Browser.

Here is one litany of complaints.Â  Nicholas Carr speaks to the issue and he recommends this summary piece, to defend his view that the internet is in some regards making our thoughts less focused and more superficial.
I've read the piece and I don't yet see the evidence.Â  There are plenty of studies where the experimenter imposes his or her own version of multitasking on the participants and then sees their performance fall.
I'm simply not convinced or even moved in my priors by these studies.Â  I can't operate a German Waschmaschine (imposed on me), and that's without an internet connection running in the background.Â  Nor would I do well if confronted by, say, the open internet windows of Brad DeLong, or his devices, whatever they may be, and in the broader scheme of things surely he counts as intellectually close to me.Â  Yet overall my life runs quite smoothly.
To sound intentionally petulant, the only multitasking that works for me is mine, mine, mine!Â  Until I see a study showing that self-chosen multi-tasking programs lower performance, I don't see that the needle has budged.
I do see stronger evidence (as cited) that video games make people more aggressive.Â  I also see overwhelming evidence that the internet gets people to read and write more.Â  The latter is probably a good thing.Â  I also believe the internet leads to less interest in long novels and more interest in non-fiction.Â  I won't judge that one, but it's misleading to cite only the decline of interest in long novels and by the way don't forget Harry Potter, the form is hardly dead.
I do, by the way, ban laptops in my smaller classes.Â  But that's paternalism, and the desire to produce a class-level publc good, not fear of my students' cognitive decline.Â  I can well imagine that they are processing more information, and doing it more effectively, when they are not listening to me, and the other students, so intently.
For extensions of my argument, see my book Create Your Own Economy, soon to be released in paperback with the new and superior title The Age of the Infovore.
title: Is multi-tasking and modern information technology bad for us?

MaybeÂ I've covered too many Paul Krugman posts lately, but since he blogged Germany, and I'm now covering Germany,Â it's worth a quick look.Â  After proposing that we get tough with the Chinese, Krugman wrote:

And itâ€™s also important to send a message to the Germans: we are not going to let them export the consequences of their obsession with austerity.
Nicely, nicely isnâ€™t working. Time to get tough.

YetÂ Germany already hasÂ passed a constitutional amendment mandating a more or less balanced budget by 2016.Â  Germany also has EU treaty obligations (admittedly, they broke them in the past, though I suspect they view those lawless days as behind them) limitingÂ the GermanÂ fiscal deficit to three percent of gdp.
Would trade sanctions on GermanyÂ lead to a trade war with the entire EU directly, or only indirectly?
There's also a distinction between a balanced budget and the overall level of government expenditure, the latter being quite high in Germany.Â  The German government spends a lot of money, in various ways, putting people to work.Â  It's called the city of Berlin!Â  Plus they have stronger automatic stabilizers than does the U.S..Â  Deficits are not the only tool of job promotion or aggregateÂ demand promotion.
Germany also transfers a good bit of money (or for that matter political capital) to the poorer EU nations and in that manner boosts global consumption.Â  Not to mention the billions the country has borrowed and spent, designed to turn the Ossis into permanent consumers, including at a global level.
Germany, unlike China,Â has not been engaging in currency manipulation.Â  In large part German exports are so high because Germany is a productive economy, with quality outputs well geared to world markets.Â  There are plenty of fiscally austere countries, at various points in time, which do not have Germany's track record of export success.
You can make anÂ argument that bundling with some weaker countries has artificially lowered the value of the German currency.Â  ButÂ even now the Euro is stronger than the deutschmark had been and in that sense Germany gave its currency an artificial boost, the opposite of what China has been doing.
It seems that Krugman is interested in helping the U.S.Â through a get tough measure. On another front, Germany is finding itselfÂ unableÂ to much control the fiscal policies of Greece and they have entered in a common political union with a (supposedly) binding fiscal rule.Â  Germany also has numerous European countries on its side in its struggle with Greece and is much larger, relative to Greece, than the United States is to Germany.Â  If Germany can't control the fiscal policy of Greece, how much can we control Germany?

I've heard (non-serious) talk that Germany should leave the Eurozone instead of Greece.Â  The Euro would then fall in value and all would be better, supposedly.
That makes some logical sense, but I don't think it can work that way.Â  Let's say the new DM-euro currency would suddenly be worth fifteen percent more than the now-depreciated new euro.Â  Everyone would want to claim that their "old euros" should count as DM-euros and it would be very hard to suddenly introduce a border-defined scheme of money stamping.Â  The problem would be Germany's to solve.Â  Yes they could survive a massive inflow of currency from around the Eurozone (presumably checked by bank holidays elsewhere), but why would they wish to court it?Â  Furthermore they have to count on the other countries to get the bank holidays right, which is likely but hardly certain.
Alternatively, let's say the new Drachma-euro is suddenly worth fifteen or twenty percent less.Â  Logically that's quite similar to the first case.Â  Now Greek currency holders would all wish to claim they had "old, real Euros, not the new silly Drachma-euros."Â  Stamping doesn't arrive quickly enough to demarcate a difference.Â  Currency will flow out of Greece, and maybe that's bad, but it's Greece's problem not Germany's problem.Â  Greek-held currency is too small to create a big problem for Germany or elsewhere.
The Germans will strongly prefer that the Greeks leave the currency union and indeed that is how they talk.
On top of that issue, Austria, Benelux and France all pegged to the German mark, with varying degrees of strictness, for some time before the introduction of the euro.Â  They will want to go with Germany and indeed they probably should go with Germany.Â  The scenario of "Germany leaving" raises the awkward question of why won't they go too and how to coordinate the entire shift.
One way or another, Greece leaves first, if indeed the Eurozone breaks up.
title: Does Germany or Greece leave the Euro first?

text:
SomeÂ of you thought that I was making fun of Germans by scrutinizing one of the local newspapers, the Berliner Morgenpost.Â  Quite the contrary, the paper is more sophisticated than its American equivalents and furthermore I enjoy reading it myself.Â  What I am making fun of is people who have unrealistic expectations of how Germany can be slotted into this or that academic plan, without recognizing the realities of national and regionalÂ cultures.
Other people have suggested that Die Zeit or the FAZ are more representative of German opinion.Â  Among elites for sure, but if youÂ walk through Berlin for days you will see the Berliner Morgenpost for sale much more often, by an order of magnitude.
Anyway, I noticed aÂ piece in the 12 June edition, entitled "Germany is driving European economic growth."Â Â What's most striking about thie article, and other sources, is how muchÂ Keynesianism hasÂ failed to influence either German policy or German public opinion.Â  In the piece, there is no mention of international imbalances or aggregate demand issues, but rather Germany is lauded for exporting so much and for serving as the economic locomotive forÂ European economic activity.Â Â Furthermore this is a news story, not an Op-Ed.
Germany, of course, is one of the most successfulÂ countriesÂ in the world since its postwar reconstruction.Â  (You could make a good case for giving Germany the "best country award" for the last fifty or sixty years.)Â  Yet German policymakers adhere reasonably consistently to the followingÂ views:
1. It is the long run which matters and we should be obsessed with the long run consequences of our choices.
2. Economic growth comes from highÂ productivity, most of allÂ in quality manufacturing.
3. Borrowing to finance consumption is a nicht-nicht.Â  Savings is all-important.
4. If we need to make a big change, we'll all grit our teeth and do it.Â  For instance Germany has done a good deal, on the real side,Â to restore its export competitiveness in the last ten years, not to mention unification and postwar recovery. 
5. These strictures should be enforced by rigorous rules, to limit temptation, because indeed you will find cases where it appears to make sense to break the rules.Â Â 
6. Values matter, as do norms of cooperation.
7. Don't obsess over the creation of too many low-wage jobs, because in the longer run it will be bad for your cultural capital.Â  If need be, pay people to be unemployed, but hold high human capital.Â  In the longer run, try to educate them up to higher productivity and thus employment.
8. Be obsessedÂ with self-improvement, most of all at the personal level.
(If you're wondering, the recent talk about coalition collapse is not challenging these basic principles.Â  There is talk about not cutting some kinds of government spending, or raising taxes on the wealthy, or whether the ruling coalition can get things done, or whether the draft should be abolished, or whether Germany has mishandled the Euro crisis.Â  German politics produces a lot of government spending, and that is part of the above vision, but there is a great concernÂ about whether it is paid for in the proper way.)
Most Keynesian economics makes goodÂ sense to me, especially at the methodological level.Â  But when it comes to principles for guiding a countryâ€¦?Â  TheÂ numbered items above areÂ not exactly my preferred list (especially not for the United States), butÂ they haveÂ worked out very well for Germany.Â  I would not so lightly toss them away.Â  Might these principles be better, all things considered, than the Keynesian alternatives?
I'm aÂ fan of the northern European social democracies, but in part they succeedÂ because those countries don't follow all of the prescriptions you might hear coming from their boosters in theÂ United States.Â  For instance American liberals often admire the activist government in such countries, but it's built upon a very different set of cultural foundations.Â  I hear or readÂ liberals calling for the comparable interventions but usually remaining quiteÂ silent about the accompanying cultural foundations or in some cases actively opposing them.
The cultural elements of the current Keynesian debates remain underexplored in the United States, but they are fairly well understood in Germany.
title: No Keynesianism in the Berliner Morgenpost

You'll see so many blog posts and columns talking aboutÂ the low interest rates and high unemployment of our times, thus arguing in favor ofÂ further fiscal stimulus.
So far, these are the least likely arguments you will hear addressed:
1. The monetary authority moves last anyway.
2. We don't need exotic "quantitative easing," we can simply print up more money and hand it out to consumers through a simple vouchers program, at basically zero budgetary cost.Â  If consumers save all that money, fiscal stimulus also won't have much of a kick.
3. The real fiscal problem is spending contraction at the state level (expanding and contracting spending are not symmetric in their effects; contracting spend hurts more than expanding spending helps).Â  The correct fiscal policy move would have been, and still is, to take Medicaid away from the states and make it fully federal.Â  This would give state budgets a huge break, and help employment, yet asÂ a one-timeÂ changeÂ it reducesÂ the moral hazard problems from ongoing outright grants.Â Â Furthermore federalizing Medicaid is a good idea in its own right and it also could be a spur to make other improvements in the program.
4. Rather than just arguing about the most likely scenario, we should apply the same worst case scenario thinking that is recommended for climate change.
5. Macroeconomics really is just a theory.Â  Politicians are reluctant to spend more money, in tough times, on the basis of a mere theory.Â  Advocates of fiscal stimulus make it sound as simple as solving an undergraduateÂ homework problem and I think they sometimes genuinely do not realize how much the rest of the world, including politicians,Â views them as simply being very convinced by their own theory.Â  There are plenty of historical examples with confounding factors and I've linked to some of them lately.Â Â One default hypothesis isÂ that the ranges of fiscal policy being discussed, whether looser or tighter, aren't going to matter much one way or the other.Â Â 
The next time you read a blog post or column on fiscal stimulus, and it isn't addressing those issues, the correct response is to think that a deeper analysis is needed.Â  Don't be swayed by the mere repetition of the usual arguments about interest rates, unemployment rates, and the like.

As a scandinavian I'm surprised by the admiration for Germany. 
We often talk of Germany as being a step behind in economic policy with their labor market being so rigid, and the still significant power of unions. 

When I first visited West Germany, in 1985, it was arguably the best-functioning social democracy.Â  You could mail a letterÂ for single-day delivery anywhere in the Bundesrepublik, the concept of "deutsche Wertarbeit" was near its peak, Mercedes was the gold standard of automobiles, and the northwest industrial areas had not yet been hollowed out (though they were suffering).Â  The country also had among the world's best systems for mass transit and urban planning, as well a high living standard and lots of vacation time, all topped off by what was arguably the world's most curious, most travel-hungry, and most intellectual population.
Since then, unification cost a lot of money, and delayed progress, but the country hasn't exactly fallen apart.Â  It retains many of these virtues, albeit with some fraying at the edges.Â  What it has gained since 1985 is a greater feeling of normalcy, a stronger identity as European, much better levels of customer service, and the final aging and (mostly) disappearance of a large number of Nazis and Nazi sympathizers.Â  Those who were sixty, and running the country, are now eighty-five and mostly dead or retired.Â  Those are some big gains.
The Nordic countries have in some ways moved ahead.Â  The stunning contemporary architecture of CopenhagenÂ sets the city apart from most of Germany, which now has a somewhat tired-looking infrastructure and a great number of mediocre postwar buildings. Via Menzie Chinn, Mark CopelovichÂ writes:

As the Fund's largest quota contributors, the "G-5" countries (the US, Germany, Japan, UK, and France) exercise de facto control over IMF lending decisions. At the same time, the G-5 countries are also home to the largest private creditors in global markets, including the world's largest commercial banks. Consequently, G-5 bank exposure heavily influences these governments' preferences over IMF lending policies. In particular, I find that IMF loan size and conditionality vary widely based on the intensity and heterogeneity of G-5 governments' domestic financial ties to a particular borrower country. When private lenders throughout the G-5 countries are highly exposed to a borrower country, G-5 governments collectively have intense preferences and are more likely to approve larger IMF loans with relatively limited conditionality. In contrast, when G-5 private creditors' exposure to a country is smaller or more unevenly distributed, G-5 governments' interests are weaker and less cohesive, and the Fund approves smaller loans with more extensive conditionality. I find strong evidence that these patterns hold both within countries over time (I focus on IMF lending to Korea and Mexico from 1983-1997 in the book), as well as more systematically over time and across cases for the universe of IMF loans from 1984-2003.

Read the whole thing;Â my original post was here.Â Â 
On my point 1, that the central bank moves last, Brad writes:

Yes, the central bank can neutralize any additional fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates. (It is not clear that it can undo any fiscal contraction by some combination of lowering interest rates and quantitative easing: it may be able to.) What is clear is that the U.S. Federal Reserve and the Bank of England are right now definitely not in a place where they would neutralize any additional fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates. And my bet is that the ECB is also not in such a placeâ€“although it is much harder to figure out what they think and what they will do. That the central bank moves last is important and relevant, but not determinative when you are in the neighborhood of the zero lower bound on interest rates.

Maybe the central bank cannot undo a fiscal tightening, but surely it can undo a fiscal expansion, by making money tighter,Â limiting QE, and/or changing the pace at which it undoes previous QE.Â  My assumption is that the central bank has a preferred inflation vs. unemployment position for the economy, so why be so sure they won't undo the expansion of the fiscal authority, if only probabilistically?Â  Portfolio considerations, or public relations, may matter, so I am not postulating strict neutrality, ratherÂ changes in fiscal debt do less good than we might think.Â Â Â 
OnÂ point two, that monetary expansion is easy, even at the zero bound, Brad writes:

That's why having the government hire unemployed people to do useful things and paying for it by printing up money at basically zero budgetary cost (right now) is an even better policy. Even if consumers do save all that money, fiscal stimulus on the spending side still has an impact: useful stuff gets done.

That's fine,Â with the side note that I am more skeptical aboutÂ public sector spending.Â  I'll push this line of reasoning to the next step, however, and stress we don't need to increase debt at all to have a big and effective stimulus.Â  (By the way, accepting thisÂ argument means that a central bank can undoÂ a decrease in the federal debt, as mentionedÂ in point one.)Â Â Â  
OnÂ point three, on federalizing Medicaid,Â we agree.Â Â Point four is about the value ofÂ worst-case thinking and that means a fiscal crisis can come even when it appears unlikely.Â  I wish to heed that risk by doing something other than pledgingÂ our next President and Congress will solve the problem.
Elsewhere, Brad has written:

The obvious policy is the long-term debt neutral stimulus: spending increases and tax cuts for the next three years, standby tax increases with triggers and spending caps with triggers thereafter, all calculated to guarantee that the debt is no larger ten years from now than in the baseline.

An alternativeÂ version of this would be:

We can and should do major stimulus without increasing the debt burden, short-term or long-term.Â  Increasing M, through monetary policy, is usually more effective than making periodic attempts to keep V up and running, through fiscal policy.Â  Plus it is often easier to turn monetary rather than fiscal policyÂ on a dime, especially in a democracy and for Brad I can cite the risk of a Republican administration.Â  Talk of the zero bound doesn't matter much for the policies we should choose, namely money-financed, non-exoticÂ direct stimulus.

Why is it necessary to take on or intellectually defend higher debt levels?Â  Short-term debt can too easily become a long-term commitment.Â  Why is it necessary to discuss the zero bound so much?Â Â In my view of this exchange, Brad and I largely agree, but he does not (yet?) agree that we largely agree.Â  I want to see him criticize debt finance more than he seems willing to do.
I believe the "zero bound" is perhaps the single largest "red herring" in the economics profession today.

Under the current system, kidneys are allocated to patients primarily based on the time that the patient has been on the waiting list and the quality of the match.Â  If we evaluate these criteria "locally" there's nothing obviously wrong but if we step back and think globally, that is think about what the ultimate goal of the transplant system should be, then the current system is deeply misguided.Â  Suppose that we want the transplant system to maximize total life expectancy or, as it is known in the literature, to maximize the life-years from transplant (LYFT).
The current system does not maximize life expectancy.Â  In the current system, a 60 year old patient can be given a 20 year old kidneyâ€“that's a waste because the life expectancy of the kidney is longer than that of the patient; it's like putting a new clutch in a car that is rusting away.Â  If we had 20 year-old kidneys to spare, this wouldn't be a big problem.Â  But we don't have 20-year old kidneys to spare, so we also give 20-year old patients 60-year old kidneys which means the kidney is likely to die early taking the patient along with it.Â  If we want to maximize total life expectancy, younger people should get younger kidneys.

 It's not just age that matters, it turns out that the longer a patient has been on dialysis the less is their life expectancy after transplant (dialysis stresses the body so the sooner we get someone a transplant the better).Â  Although it may seem unfair, if we want to maximize total life expectancy we are doing the wrong thing by giving more points to patients who have been on the list longer.Â Â 
An optimized allocation system that took into account these considerations would increase total life
expectancy (modestly but significantly, about 11,500 extra life years) but it wouldn't benefit every individual.Â  Maximizing life expectancy would shift organs away from older people and people who have been on the waiting list a long time towards younger people.Â  As a result, some patients have argued that LYFT is unfair.Â  The Office of Civil Rights is even asking whether LYFT might violate age discrimination laws.Â Â 
But consider, would the older patients have objected to LYFT when they were younger?Â  If not, shouldn't their objections be discounted?Â  More formally, consider how people would vote behind a veil of ignorance.Â  By definition a LYFT approach maximizes total life expectancy, so without knowing the specifics of who you are or when you might need a transplant it's likely that behind a veil of ignorance just about everyone would favor LYFT.Â  Thus, in my view LYFT is a fair and ethical system.Â 
Here are previous MR posts on kidney transplant policy.
title: Optimizing Kidney Allocation: LYFT for LIFE

Keep in mind that unemployment rates today are disproportionately concentrated in low-income and low-education workers.Â  Haven't we been told, for years, that these same individuals are seeing some mix of stagnant and eroding wages?Â  That they are experiencing downward mobility?Â  That the real value of health care benefits has been falling and that more and more jobs don't offer health care benefits at all?Â  
Doesn't that meanâ€¦umâ€¦their wages aren't so sticky downwards?Â  And thus Keynesian economics is not the final story?
Or take illegal immigrant Mexican construction workers, a group which lost jobs in large numbers following the crash.Â  Are they â€” who often came from $1 a day environments â€“Â also supposed to have sticky wages?Â  They are out of work in massive numbers.Â  A lot of them went back home, which is a sign they are willing to make major adjustments.Â  It simply may beÂ they were no longer employable in the United States at any plausible wage.
The alternative model is that many low-education workersÂ are not employable through marginal changes in current conditions.Â  It may require a bigÂ upward Schwung for the entire chain of labor, so that desperate employers at the bottom of the ladder, unable to find anyone else,Â grudgingly hire these not-so-productive individuals because there is no other way of expanding.Â  In other words, it requires conditions which raise the marginal value product of these workers to the private sector, keeping in mind that the fixed costs of hiring a worker mostly have been going up due to the greater bureaucratization of society.
Under this hypothesis, the stimulus that works in the short-run is direct government employment of low-skilled labor, not funneling money through private contracting, and hoping the unemployed get picked up.
What should the government do with these workers?Â  Does their direct employment conflict with the Davis-Bacon Act or other regulations?Â  What wage should we pay to make sure we don't drain off workers from private sector jobs?Â  How much longer does it take such forms of stimulus to result in sustainable, private sector jobs?
As you'll see in my Principles text with Alex, we both believe that wage stickiness (both nominal and real) is a genuine issue in market settings, even in the absence of government intervention.Â  Still, I'm not convinced stickiness is the major problem today, at least not in a simple, direct manner.
If there is going to be more U.S. stimulus, it's exact nature should be thought through very carefully.Â  It's an additional question whether ourÂ politics is up to that.
title: How sticky are wages today anyway?

Paris has dozens of restaurants which are better than any in Berlin, and then hundreds more better than the rest.Â  Yet it may be the case that you have, overall, a better food life in Berlin than in Paris.
Berlin has a weakÂ reputation among foodies, but culinary life in the cityÂ is much improved.Â  Here are my tips forÂ a good eating life in Berlin:
1. Find aÂ steady source of innovative rolls, buns,Â and dark breads.Â  These are the glories of Berlin and in many parts of town there will be at least one such source per residential block.Â  The more irregular the colors, seeds, and topologies of the breads, the more enthusiastically you should buy them.Â  Do not treat this as the French bread buying experience.
2. Find a source for good spreads, such as cherry, raspberry, etc. and stock up.Â  Repeatedly apply the spreadsÂ to the breads, until death of the researcherÂ intervenes.Â  This procedureÂ is the basis for everything else you will do.Â  It ensuresÂ that allÂ of your food days will beÂ good ones.
3. Seek out mid-level German restaurants, of the kind promoted in the Time Out Guide;Â Renger-Patzsch is a good example.Â  The vegetables in such places will be consistently excellent.
4. The speed and service quality of most meals will be much better if you arrive before 7 p.m.
5. Don't obsess over German food.Â  It's underrated, but stillÂ a lot of it isn't that good.Â  In Berlin, and many other parts of Germany, you have first-class delicatessens or stores with foodstuffs from France, Italy, and many other parts of the world.Â  Use them.Â  Berlin offers one of the best overall selections in this regard, better thanÂ New York City or Paris, for instance, in terms of real access.Â  You can eatÂ first-rate French cheese every day.
6. When it comes to Berlin German food, don't eat anything in a sauce.Â  It will be either boring or disgusting.Â  Sorry.
7. The sausage spread at the KaDeWe (make sure you live near that place) is probably the best in the entire world.Â  Go there regularly.Â  They also have first-rate sausages from France, Spain, and other countries, as well as an unparalleled selection of sausages from the different regions of Germany, organized one region per case.Â  This food source, like #1, insures that each of your food days will be a splendid one.
8. Go to Berlin's numerous and varied ethnic restaurants, especially in the slightly lower rent districts.Â  If the food is supposed to be spicy, you must repeat the following incantation several times: "Ich will es essen, genau wie Sie es zu Hause essen.Â  Ich bin kein deutscher."Â  [I wantÂ to eat it exactly as you eat it at home.Â  I am not a German."]Â  Repeat especially that last part: "Ich bin kein deutscher."Â  Repeat it even if you are a German.Â  This will usually work and typically your Chinese or Thai or Indian server will smile and laughÂ in response.Â  If they view you as a German, you are screwed no matter what.Â  Simply asking for the food to be "spicy" or even "very spicy" is laughable.Â  It is showing yourself to be a fool and a sucker.
9.Â Food here is much cheaper than in Paris, and it is much easier to get into virtually any restaurant.Â  Take advantage of both features.
10. Italian food here is almost always reasonably good, and reasonably cheap, but it is rarely great.Â  Lots of cream sauces.Â  It's a good enough fall back and you find it virtually everywhere.Â  A quite good pasta for $6 or even less is a common experience.Â  Sometimes it's actually German food in disguise, or not in disguise, such as when you get Carpaccio with Pfifferlinge.
11. For ethnic food, I recommendÂ the following: Tian Fu in Wilmersdorf (very good Sichuan), Suriya-Kanthi (Sri Lankan in Prenzlauer Berg),Â Genazvale (Georgian food in Charlottenburg), Degirman is one good Turkish place of many, a slew of authentic Mexican restaurantsÂ (more than in Virginia), DAO restaurant in Charlottenburg (Thai food, best papaya salad I've had, all-around excellent), and Schneeweiss has first-rateÂ Wiener Schnitzel.
Overall Sri Lankan and Nepalese and East bloc cuisines areÂ better here, or more available, than in the USA.
If you visit for one day, you won't be so impressed with culinary life in Berlin.Â  If you stay for a month, you won't want to go back to what you had before.
title: How to eat well in Berlin

One summary of the detailsÂ is hereÂ (I don't know whateverÂ inside story there may be), but the bottom line is that he had to resign from The Washington PostÂ because of negative comments he made about conservative figures on a supposedly private email list.Â  Weigel's job for the Post was to cover the conservative movement and it seems the Post expected him to maintain a more objective stance, includingÂ in his private emails.Â  Matt Yglesias has more extensive coverage of the episode and here is Ross Douthat.Â  Here is Weigel's account and apology, which includes the postings which got him into trouble.Â  And here is a detailed Politico article.
It isÂ likely I prefer Weigel over his replacement, and if you're wondering I don'tÂ know Weigel well, even though he lives nearby.
At a more general level this is a tax on journalists, who now have a greater fear of being fired for past actions.Â  It's also a tax on the moody, the volatile, the web-savvy, the non-mainstream, and a subsidy to in-control smooth talkers and careful writers.
The Washington Post wrote:

â€œBut weâ€™re living in an era when maybe we need to add a levelâ€� of inquiry, he [a WP web site managing editor] said. â€œIt may be in our interests to ask potential reporters: â€˜In privateâ€¦ have you expressed any opinions that would make it difficult for you to do your job.â€�

I'm not sure what kind of answers they expect to that question nor what they understand by the word "private" in that context.Â  
Conceptually, the core problem is that the distinction between the private and public spheres is breaking down, but at different rates for individuals and mainstream institutions.Â  The practical question is what an equilibrium would look like for the WP, given that the paper courts advertisers, relies on political contacts, and wishes to avoid becoming a target for right-wing (and left-wing) media.Â  It's easy to imagine the targets ofÂ Weigel's criticisms citing them repeatedly against the Washington Post and questioning the Post's objectivity.Â  "Oh, that was written by the guy who said thatâ€¦"
One possible outcome is that the current public code of behaviorÂ becomes applied to writers' private lives and I suppose that is what we are seeing and it is also what a lot of "common knowledge" models would predict.Â  That is, most of us know thatÂ many writers say such things in private, but that's tolerated as long as it doesn't become common knowledgeÂ about any particular writer.
Common knowledge mechanisms often lead toÂ inefficient (and unfair) outcomes, in partÂ by non-convexying returns with regard to the actions of the individual.Â  Maybe we would like taxes to be linked to individual type, but common knowledge mechanisms tend to link the actual "tax" to how social forces process information about an individual.Â  A polemicist who is secretly taped encounters a greatly different outcome.than a polemicist who is not taped.
One option is for public institutions to adopt aÂ "statute of limitations" for private remarks and with a short time window.Â  That would not help in this case, since Weigel's relevant postings do not predate his Post employment; still it might be a good reform.Â Â Another option is for public institutions to adopt different norms for their web writers.Â  There are already different norms to some extent (web writings receive less editing, for instance), but it is hard to spread the different norm for the writing to become a different norm for the writer.Â  Web traffic is already massive for newspapers, and most readers probably do not distinguish between different kinds of paper employees, such as web vs. non-web.Â  Anyway, it's a fuzzy line if a writer has both web and non-web output.
A more radical change would move away from the manufactured image ofÂ the objective newspaper, but this isÂ especially difficultÂ for the Post, given that it relies on both conservative and liberal sources for its key political coverage.
Overall, we need more incentive-compatible, generalizableÂ organizational reforms which will allow mainstreamÂ institutionsÂ to have more flexible relationships, and indeed sometimes more distanced relationships,Â with their writers.Â  Yet reputational forces are often quite blunt, and grossly calculated, and mainstream institutions areÂ not very far along on making such reforms work.
title: The Dave Weigel resignation

The unfolding of the financial crisis has also changed the publicâ€™s sense of where change is needed, both in the United States and Europe. Brad DeLong discusses a recent short essay by Kartik Athreya; Matt Yglesias chips in, as does Scott Sumner.
My view is a little different than Brad's.Â  I would say that economics is really, really, really, really, really, really, really hard.Â  And that's leaving out a few of theÂ "reallys."
It's so hard that experts don't always do it well.Â Â The expertsÂ are constantly prone to correction by non-experts, by practitioners, by people who are self-educated economic experts but not professional economists, and by people who know some economics and a lot about some other field(s).Â  It is very often that we â€” at least some of us â€“Â are wrong and at least some of those other people are right.Â  Furthermore those other people are often more meta-rational than a lot of professional economists.
Even very simple problems can be quite hard, such as why nominal wages are sometimes sticky or why particular markets don't always clear, in the absence of legal impediment.Â  Why doesn't the restaurant charge more on a Saturday night?Â  You can imagine how hard the hard problems are, such as what level of public expenditure is consistent with an ongoing and workableÂ democratic equilibrium.
Putting aside agreement and ideology, and just focusing on how one understands an issue, I'll take my favorite non-Ph.d. bloggers over most professional economists, six out of seven days a week.Â Â Not to estimate a coefficient, but to judge public policy, thereby integrating and evaluating broad bodies of knowledge?Â  It's not even close.
